records.source: וַיְהִי֙ כִּֽי־זָקֵ֣ן יִצְחָ֔ק וַתִּכְהֶ֥יןָ עֵינָ֖יו מֵרְאֹ֑ת וַיִּקְרָ֞א אֶת־עֵשָׂ֣ו׀בְּנ֣וֹ הַגָּדֹ֗ל וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ בְּנִ֔י וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו הִנֵּֽנִי׃
records.gloss: And it was, when was old Isaac and grew dim his eyes from seeing, and he called Esau his son the elder and said to him, my son; and he said to him, here I [am].
pieces: Isaac had grown old, and his sight had faded until he could no longer see. He sent for Esau, the older of his two sons, and said, "My son!" "Yes, I am here," Esau answered.

L.1: And it came about, when Isaac was old and his eyes were too dim to see, that he called Esau his elder son and said to him, "My son." And he said to him, "Here I am."

R.1: Isaac was now old, and he had become blind. One day he called his older son Esau. "My son," he said. "Yes, Father," Esau answered.

decisions.choice: his eyes were too dim to see: Isaac is nearly or wholly blind
decisions.reason: The whole story turns on this. Isaac must judge by voice, touch, taste and smell (verses 21-27), and each of them is deceived. The same verb is used of the failing sight of the old priest Eli (1 Samuel 3:2).

decisions.choice: his elder son: literally "his big son"
decisions.reason: The words "big" and "small" (gadol, qatan) are used for the older and younger son (verses 15, 42). Before the twins were born, God said "the older will serve the younger" (25:23).

decisions.choice: here I am: ready to listen and obey
decisions.reason: The usual answer to a call, as Abraham's in 22:1 and 22:11. It means "I am listening; what do you want?"

decisions.choice: Yes, I am here (B); Yes, Father (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the reply (m3) in the way a son would answer.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּה־נָ֖א זָקַ֑נְתִּי לֹ֥א יָדַ֖עְתִּי י֥וֹם מוֹתִֽי׃
records.gloss: And he said, look, please, I am old; not I know [the] day of my death.
pieces: "I am an old man now," Isaac said, "and any day could be my last.

L.2: And he said, "Look now, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.

R.2: Isaac said, "I am very old. I could die any day.

decisions.choice: I do not know the day of my death: I may die at any time
decisions.reason: Isaac speaks as a man preparing for death and wanting to settle the blessing while he can. In fact he lives many more years: Jacob comes back to him twenty years later (31:41; 35:27-29).

decisions.choice: any day could be my last (B); I could die any day (R)
alternatives: I do not know the day of my death
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the expression (m1).

records.source: וְעַתָּה֙ שָׂא־נָ֣א כֵלֶ֔יךָ תֶּלְיְךָ֖ וְקַשְׁתֶּ֑ךָ וְצֵא֙ הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה וְצ֥וּדָה לִּ֖י צָֽיִד׃
records.gloss: And now take up, please, your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out [to] the field and hunt for me game.
pieces: So take your hunting things, your quiver and your bow, and go out into the open country and bring down some wild game for me.

L.3: Now then, please take up your gear, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me,

R.3: Take your bow and arrows and go out into the fields. Hunt a wild animal for me.

decisions.choice: your gear (kelim), your quiver: hunting equipment
decisions.reason: Kelim is a general word for equipment or weapons. The word for "quiver" (teli) occurs only here; it may mean a quiver or a sword hung at the side. The sense is clear: Esau is to take what he needs to hunt.

decisions.choice: game: the marginal spelling of the word
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew spells the word for game with an extra letter; the Masoretes' marginal reading gives the usual spelling (tsayid). The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: the field: the open country beyond the settled land
decisions.reason: Esau is "a man of the field", a skilled hunter (25:27), and his father loved the game he brought home (25:28).

records.source: וַעֲשֵׂה־לִ֨י מַטְעַמִּ֜ים כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָהַ֛בְתִּי וְהָבִ֥יאָה לִּ֖י וְאֹכֵ֑לָה בַּעֲב֛וּר תְּבָרֶכְךָ֥ נַפְשִׁ֖י בְּטֶ֥רֶם אָמֽוּת׃
records.gloss: and prepare for me tasty food such as I love, and bring [it] to me, that I may eat, so that may bless you my soul before I die.
pieces: and cook it into the savory dish I am fond of. Bring it to me to eat, so that I can give you my blessing myself before I die."

L.4: and prepare me tasty food such as I love, and bring it to me, so that I may eat, in order that my soul may bless you before I die."

R.4: Cook it the way I like it best and bring it to me. After I eat it, I will bless you before I die."

decisions.choice: my soul may bless you: I myself may bless you
alternatives: that I may bless you with all my heart
decisions.reason: Nefesh, often translated "soul", here stands for the whole person: "I myself". It may also carry the warmth of a blessing given from deep within.

decisions.choice: blessing before death: a father's last words to his sons
decisions.reason: A dying father's blessing passed on the family's future and was thought to carry real power, which could not be taken back once spoken (verses 33, 37). Jacob later blesses his own sons before he dies (chapter 49).

decisions.choice: tasty food (mat'ammim): a dish with a good flavor
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "to taste". Food prepared for the occasion goes with the blessing; a meal often sealed solemn words (26:30).

decisions.choice: my soul may bless you
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew expression (m1); Balanced has "I ... myself".

records.source: וְרִבְקָ֣ה שֹׁמַ֔עַת בְּדַבֵּ֣ר יִצְחָ֔ק אֶל־עֵשָׂ֖ו בְּנ֑וֹ וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ עֵשָׂו֙ הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה לָצ֥וּד צַ֖יִד לְהָבִֽיא׃
records.gloss: And Rebekah [was] listening when spoke Isaac to Esau his son. And went Esau [to] the field to hunt game to bring [it].
pieces: Now Rebekah had been listening while Isaac talked to their son Esau. So when Esau went off to the open country to hunt game and bring it back,

L.5: And Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt game [and] to bring [it].

R.5: Rebekah was listening while Isaac spoke to Esau. As soon as Esau left to go hunting,

decisions.choice: Esau his son: Isaac's son, as Jacob is "her son" (verse 6)
decisions.reason: The narrator calls Esau Isaac's son and Jacob Rebekah's son, recalling 25:28: "Isaac loved Esau ... but Rebekah loved Jacob." The family is divided.

decisions.choice: So when Esau went off ... (verse 6 completes the sentence)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join Esau's leaving to Rebekah's action in verse 6, to show that she acts at once.

records.source: וְרִבְקָה֙ אָֽמְרָ֔ה אֶל־יַעֲקֹ֥ב בְּנָ֖הּ לֵאמֹ֑ר הִנֵּ֤ה שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־אָבִ֔יךָ מְדַבֵּ֛ר אֶל־עֵשָׂ֥ו אָחִ֖יךָ לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And Rebekah said to Jacob her son, saying, look, I heard your father speaking to Esau your brother, saying,
pieces: Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "Listen. I overheard your father telling your brother Esau,

L.6: And Rebekah said to Jacob her son, "Look, I heard your father speaking to Esau your brother, saying,

R.6: she said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father talking to your brother Esau. He said,

records.source: הָבִ֨יאָה לִּ֥י צַ֛יִד וַעֲשֵׂה־לִ֥י מַטְעַמִּ֖ים וְאֹכֵ֑לָה וַאֲבָרֶכְכָ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י מוֹתִֽי׃
records.gloss: bring for me game and prepare for me tasty food, that I may eat, and I will bless you before YHWH before my death.
pieces: 'Bring me some game and make me a tasty meal. After I have eaten I will bless you in the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} before I die.'

L.7: 'Bring me game and prepare me tasty food, so that I may eat and bless you before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} before my death.'

R.7: 'Bring me an animal from your hunt and cook it for me. After I eat it, I will bless you in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} before I die.'

decisions.choice: before the LORD: the blessing is spoken in God's presence
decisions.reason: Rebekah's report adds these words to what Isaac said (verse 4). They make the stakes clear: the blessing is a solemn act before God and cannot be undone.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֥ה בְנִ֖י שְׁמַ֣ע בְּקֹלִ֑י לַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֖י מְצַוָּ֥ה אֹתָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And now, my son, listen to my voice, to what I [am] commanding you.
pieces: Now, my son, do exactly as I tell you.

L.8: And now, my son, listen to my voice, to what I am commanding you.

R.8: So, my son, listen to me and do what I say.

decisions.choice: listen to my voice: obey me
decisions.reason: To "listen to the voice" of someone means to do what they say. Rebekah uses the words three times (verses 8, 13, 43).

records.source: לֶךְ־נָא֙ אֶל־הַצֹּ֔אן וְקַֽח־לִ֣י מִשָּׁ֗ם שְׁנֵ֛י גְּדָיֵ֥י עִזִּ֖ים טֹבִ֑ים וְאֶֽעֱשֶׂ֨ה אֹתָ֧ם מַטְעַמִּ֛ים לְאָבִ֖יךָ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָהֵֽב׃
records.gloss: Go, please, to the flock, and take for me from there two kids of [the] goats, good ones, and I will prepare them [as] tasty food for your father, such as he loves.
pieces: Go out to the flock and pick out two fine young goats for me. I will make them into the kind of savory dish your father likes.

L.9: Go now to the flock and fetch me from there two good young goats, and I will prepare them as tasty food for your father, such as he loves.

R.9: Go to the flock and bring me two of the best young goats. I will cook them the way your father likes.

decisions.choice: two good young goats: tender meat from the family's own flock
decisions.reason: Young goat could be cooked to taste like wild game. Two kids also give Rebekah the skins she needs (verse 16).

records.source: וְהֵבֵאתָ֥ לְאָבִ֖יךָ וְאָכָ֑ל בַּעֲבֻ֛ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יְבָרֶכְךָ֖ לִפְנֵ֥י מוֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And you will bring [it] to your father, and he will eat, so that he may bless you before his death.
pieces: Then you take it in to your father to eat, so that it is you he blesses before he dies."

L.10: And you shall bring it to your father, and he will eat, so that he may bless you before his death."

R.10: Then you will take it to your father. He will eat it and bless you before he dies."

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֔ב אֶל־רִבְקָ֖ה אִמּ֑וֹ הֵ֣ן עֵשָׂ֤ו אָחִי֙ אִ֣ישׁ שָׂעִ֔ר וְאָנֹכִ֖י אִ֥ישׁ חָלָֽק׃
records.gloss: And said Jacob to Rebekah his mother, look, Esau my brother [is] a man hairy, and I [am] a man smooth.
pieces: But Jacob objected to his mother Rebekah. "Esau my brother is covered with hair," he said, "and my skin is smooth.

L.11: And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Look, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.

R.11: Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, "My brother Esau has hair all over his body, but my skin is smooth.

decisions.choice: hairy (sa'ir): a play on Seir, Esau's land
decisions.reason: Esau was born "like a hairy cloak" (25:25), and the word sa'ir sounds like Seir, the hill country where Esau's people later lived (32:3; 36:8).

decisions.choice: smooth (chalaq): smooth-skinned
decisions.reason: The word means smooth, and elsewhere also smooth in speech, flattering (Proverbs 5:3). Jacob's worry is only about his skin; the reader may hear more.

records.source: אוּלַ֤י יְמֻשֵּׁ֨נִי֙ אָבִ֔י וְהָיִ֥יתִי בְעֵינָ֖יו כִּמְתַעְתֵּ֑עַ וְהֵבֵאתִ֥י עָלַ֛י קְלָלָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א בְרָכָֽה׃
records.gloss: Perhaps will feel me my father, and I will be in his eyes like a mocker, and I will bring upon myself a curse and not a blessing.
pieces: Suppose my father touches me. He will see that I am making a fool of him, and I will bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing."

L.12: Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will be in his eyes like a mocker, and I will bring upon myself a curse and not a blessing."

R.12: What if my father touches me? He will know I am trying to trick him. Then he will curse me instead of blessing me."

decisions.choice: like a mocker: one who makes a fool of someone
decisions.reason: The word (meta'tea) occurs only here; a related word means to mock or make sport of someone (2 Chronicles 36:16). Jacob fears being caught, not doing wrong.

decisions.choice: a curse and not a blessing
decisions.reason: A father's curse was as weighty as his blessing. Jacob's fear sets the two words side by side, as God's promise to Abraham did (12:3).

decisions.choice: Perhaps (L), Suppose (B), What if (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word (ulay) states a fear: "it may be that".

records.source: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ אִמּ֔וֹ עָלַ֥י קִלְלָתְךָ֖ בְּנִ֑י אַ֛ךְ שְׁמַ֥ע בְּקֹלִ֖י וְלֵ֥ךְ קַֽח־לִֽי׃
records.gloss: And said to him his mother, upon me [be] your curse, my son; only listen to my voice and go, take [them] for me.
pieces: "Then let the curse be mine, my son," his mother replied. "Just do as I say. Go and get the goats for me."

L.13: And his mother said to him, "Upon me be your curse, my son; only listen to my voice, and go, fetch [them] for me."

R.13: His mother said, "My son, if you are cursed, let the curse be on me. Just do what I say. Go and get the goats for me."

decisions.choice: upon me be your curse: let me bear any curse meant for you
decisions.reason: Rebekah takes the risk on herself. She may also be confident because of what God said before the twins were born (25:23). In the end she pays a price: Jacob flees, and the text never says she saw him again.

decisions.choice: the goats
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name what Jacob is to fetch (verse 9).

records.source: וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ וַיִּקַּ֔ח וַיָּבֵ֖א לְאִמּ֑וֹ וַתַּ֤עַשׂ אִמּוֹ֙ מַטְעַמִּ֔ים כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר אָהֵ֥ב אָבִֽיו׃
records.gloss: And he went and took and brought [them] to his mother, and prepared his mother tasty food such as loved his father.
pieces: So Jacob went and got them and brought them to his mother, and she cooked a savory dish the way his father liked it.

L.14: So he went and fetched [them] and brought [them] to his mother, and his mother prepared tasty food such as his father loved.

R.14: So Jacob went and got the goats and brought them to his mother. She cooked them the way his father liked.

records.source: וַתִּקַּ֣ח רִ֠בְקָה אֶת־בִּגְדֵ֨י עֵשָׂ֜ו בְּנָ֤הּ הַגָּדֹל֙ הַחֲמֻדֹ֔ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתָּ֖הּ בַּבָּ֑יִת וַתַּלְבֵּ֥שׁ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹ֖ב בְּנָ֥הּ הַקָּטָֽן׃
records.gloss: And took Rebekah the garments of Esau her son the elder, the desirable ones, which [were] with her in the house, and she clothed Jacob her son the younger.
pieces: Then Rebekah took her older son Esau's finest clothes, which she kept in the house, and dressed her younger son Jacob in them.

L.15: And Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her elder son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son.

R.15: Then Rebekah took the best clothes of her older son Esau, which she kept at home. She put them on her younger son Jacob.

decisions.choice: the best garments: literally "the desirable ones"
decisions.reason: Chamudot means precious or choice things. These were Esau's fine clothes, perhaps kept for special days, and they carried the smell of the field (verse 27).

decisions.choice: her elder son ... her younger son
decisions.reason: The words "elder" and "younger" (literally "big" and "small") remind the reader of the birth order the blessing is about to overturn (25:23).

records.source: וְאֵ֗ת עֹרֹת֙ גְּדָיֵ֣י הָֽעִזִּ֔ים הִלְבִּ֖ישָׁה עַל־יָדָ֑יו וְעַ֖ל חֶלְקַ֥ת צַוָּארָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And the skins of the kids of the goats she put on his hands and on [the] smooth part of his neck.
pieces: She also covered his hands and the smooth skin of his neck with the goatskins.

L.16: And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.

R.16: She covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the hairy skins of the goats.

decisions.choice: the skins of the young goats: hair like Esau's
decisions.reason: Goat hair is coarse, and Esau was unusually hairy (25:25; verse 11), so the skins could pass for his arms and neck to a blind man's touch.

decisions.choice: hairy
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear why the skins were used.

records.source: וַתִּתֵּ֧ן אֶת־הַמַּטְעַמִּ֛ים וְאֶת־הַלֶּ֖חֶם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑תָה בְּיַ֖ד יַעֲקֹ֥ב בְּנָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And she gave the tasty food and the bread that she had prepared into [the] hand of Jacob her son.
pieces: Then she handed her son Jacob the savory dish and the bread she had made.

L.17: And she put the tasty food and the bread that she had prepared into the hand of Jacob her son.

R.17: Then she gave Jacob the meat and the bread she had made.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֥א אֶל־אָבִ֖יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אָבִ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הִנֶּ֔נִּי מִ֥י אַתָּ֖ה בְּנִֽי׃
records.gloss: And he went to his father and said, my father; and he said, here I [am]; who [are] you, my son?
pieces: He went in to his father and said, "Father!" "Yes," said Isaac. "Which of my sons are you?"

L.18: And he went in to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"

R.18: Jacob went to his father and said, "Father!" Isaac answered, "Yes, my son. Who are you?"

decisions.choice: who are you, my son?: Isaac is already unsure
decisions.reason: Isaac's first words are a question. The voice is not quite Esau's (verse 22), and the meal has come very quickly (verse 20).

decisions.choice: Which of my sons are you?
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out that Isaac knows he is speaking to one of his sons but not which.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶל־אָבִ֗יו אָנֹכִי֙ עֵשָׂ֣ו בְּכֹרֶ֔ךָ עָשִׂ֕יתִי כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ אֵלָ֑י קֽוּם־נָ֣א שְׁבָ֗ה וְאָכְלָה֙ מִצֵּידִ֔י בַּעֲב֖וּר תְּבָרֲכַ֥נִּי נַפְשֶֽׁךָ׃
records.gloss: And said Jacob to his father, I [am] Esau your firstborn; I have done as you told me. Arise, please, sit and eat of my game, so that may bless me your soul.
pieces: "It is Esau, your firstborn," Jacob told his father. "I have done what you asked. Please sit up and eat some of the game I caught, and then give me your blessing."

L.19: And Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please get up, sit and eat of my game, so that your soul may bless me."

R.19: Jacob told his father, "I am Esau, your oldest son. I did what you told me. Please sit up and eat some of the meat I hunted. Then bless me."

decisions.choice: I am Esau your firstborn: an outright lie
decisions.reason: Jacob claims both Esau's name and his rank. He had already bought the right of the firstborn (25:31-34); now he takes the blessing by deceit. The story does not excuse it, and Jacob will himself be deceived about an older and a younger (29:25-26).

decisions.choice: your soul may bless me
decisions.reason: As in verse 4, Literal keeps "soul" for the person himself.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִצְחָק֙ אֶל־בְּנ֔וֹ מַה־זֶּ֛ה מִהַ֥רְתָּ לִמְצֹ֖א בְּנִ֑י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֥י הִקְרָ֛ה יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ לְפָנָֽי׃
records.gloss: And said Isaac to his son, what [is] this, you have hurried to find [it], my son? And he said, because made [it] happen YHWH your God before me.
pieces: "How did you find it so fast, my son?" Isaac asked. "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God put it in my path," he answered.

L.20: And Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you found it so quickly, my son?" And he said, "Because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God made it happen for me."

R.20: Isaac asked his son, "How did you find an animal so quickly, my son?" Jacob answered, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God helped me find it."

decisions.choice: the LORD your God: Jacob uses God's name to cover his lie
decisions.reason: Jacob calls the LORD "your God", not "my God". Only after God meets him at Bethel does Jacob vow that the LORD will be his God (28:21).

decisions.choice: made it happen for me: brought it my way
decisions.reason: The verb (hiqrah) means to cause something to meet someone, the same verb used when Abraham's servant asked God to bring Rebekah to him (24:12).

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִצְחָק֙ אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֔ב גְּשָׁה־נָּ֥א וַאֲמֻֽשְׁךָ֖ בְּנִ֑י הַֽאַתָּ֥ה זֶ֛ה בְּנִ֥י עֵשָׂ֖ו אִם־לֹֽא׃
records.gloss: And said Isaac to Jacob, come near, please, that I may feel you, my son, whether you [are] this my son Esau or not.
pieces: Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Come closer, my son, and let me touch you, to know whether you really are my son Esau."

L.21: And Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, so that I may feel you, my son, whether you are really my son Esau or not."

R.21: Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Come close so I can touch you, my son. I want to know if you are really Esau."

records.source: וַיִּגַּ֧שׁ יַעֲקֹ֛ב אֶל־יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו וַיְמֻשֵּׁ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הַקֹּל֙ ק֣וֹל יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְהַיָּדַ֖יִם יְדֵ֥י עֵשָֽׂו׃
records.gloss: And drew near Jacob to Isaac his father, and he felt him and said, the voice [is the] voice of Jacob, and the hands [are the] hands of Esau.
pieces: Jacob came close to his father Isaac, who felt him and said, "It sounds like Jacob, but these hands are Esau's."

L.22: And Jacob drew near to Isaac his father, and he felt him and said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."

R.22: So Jacob went close to his father. Isaac touched him and said, "Your voice sounds like Jacob's voice. But your arms feel like Esau's arms."

decisions.choice: the voice ... the hands: Isaac's senses disagree
decisions.reason: Isaac trusts touch over hearing, and is wrong. The saying sums up the whole deception.

decisions.choice: arms
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word for hand (yad) can include the forearm, where the goatskins were (verse 16).

records.source: וְלֹ֣א הִכִּיר֔וֹ כִּֽי־הָי֣וּ יָדָ֗יו כִּידֵ֛י עֵשָׂ֥ו אָחִ֖יו שְׂעִרֹ֑ת וַֽיְבָרְכֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And not he recognized him, for were his hands like [the] hands of Esau his brother, hairy; and he blessed him.
pieces: He did not see through it, because Jacob's hands were hairy like his brother Esau's, and so he blessed him.

L.23: And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of Esau his brother; and he blessed him.

R.23: Isaac did not know it was Jacob, because his hands were hairy like Esau's. So Isaac blessed him.

decisions.choice: and he blessed him: the outcome told in advance
decisions.reason: The blessing itself is given in verses 27-29, after more questions and the meal. Hebrew narrative often states the result first and then tells how it came about. The verb could also mean a greeting, but here it most likely points ahead to the blessing.

decisions.choice: recognize (hikkir): a key word in Jacob's story
decisions.reason: The same verb returns when Jacob is asked to "recognize" Joseph's bloody robe (37:32-33) and when Judah is asked to "recognize" his seal (38:25-26). The deceiver is deceived the same way.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אַתָּ֥ה זֶ֖ה בְּנִ֣י עֵשָׂ֑ו וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אָֽנִי׃
records.gloss: And he said, you [are] this my son Esau? And he said, I [am].
pieces: "Are you truly my son Esau?" he asked again. "I am," said Jacob.

L.24: And he said, "Are you really my son Esau?" And he said, "I am."

R.24: Isaac asked again, "Are you really my son Esau?" Jacob answered, "Yes, I am."

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הַגִּ֤שָׁה לִּי֙ וְאֹֽכְלָה֙ מִצֵּ֣יד בְּנִ֔י לְמַ֥עַן תְּבָֽרֶכְךָ֖ נַפְשִׁ֑י וַיַּגֶּשׁ־לוֹ֙ וַיֹּאכַ֔ל וַיָּ֧בֵא ל֦וֹ יַ֖יִן וַיֵּֽשְׁתְּ׃
records.gloss: And he said, bring [it] near to me, that I may eat of [the] game of my son, so that may bless you my soul. And he brought [it] near to him and he ate; and he brought to him wine and he drank.
pieces: "Then serve it to me," Isaac said, "so that I may eat my son's game and give you my blessing." Jacob set the food before him, and he ate. He also brought him wine, and he drank.

L.25: And he said, "Bring it near to me, so that I may eat of my son's game, in order that my soul may bless you." And he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.

R.25: Isaac said, "Bring me the meat you hunted, my son. I will eat it and then bless you." So Jacob brought it to him, and Isaac ate. Jacob brought him wine too, and he drank it.

decisions.choice: wine: part of a solemn meal
decisions.reason: Rebekah's plan said nothing of wine; Jacob adds it. Bread and wine went with solemn moments of blessing (14:18).

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו יִצְחָ֣ק אָבִ֑יו גְּשָׁה־נָּ֥א וּשְׁקָה־לִּ֖י בְּנִֽי׃
records.gloss: And said to him Isaac his father, come near, please, and kiss me, my son.
pieces: Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come here, my son, and kiss me."

L.26: And Isaac his father said to him, "Please come near and kiss me, my son."

R.26: Then his father Isaac said, "Come here, my son, and kiss me."

decisions.choice: kiss me: a sign of love, and a last test
decisions.reason: A kiss was the normal greeting of family members (29:11, 13; 33:4). It also brings Jacob close enough for Isaac to smell his clothes (verse 27).

records.source: וַיִּגַּשׁ֙ וַיִּשַּׁק־ל֔וֹ וַיָּ֛רַח אֶת־רֵ֥יחַ בְּגָדָ֖יו וַֽיְבָרֲכֵ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר רְאֵה֙ רֵ֣יחַ בְּנִ֔י כְּרֵ֣יחַ שָׂדֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֵּרֲכ֖וֹ יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And he came near and kissed him, and he smelled [the] smell of his garments and blessed him and said, see, [the] smell of my son [is] like [the] smell of a field that has blessed it YHWH.
pieces: So he came close and kissed him, and when Isaac caught the smell of his clothes, he blessed him: "Ah, my son smells like open country that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has blessed!

L.27: And he came near and kissed him; and he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has blessed.

R.27: Jacob went close and kissed him. When Isaac smelled Esau's clothes on him, he blessed him. He said, "My son smells like a field that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has blessed.

decisions.choice: the smell of his garments: Esau's clothes, smelling of the open country
decisions.reason: Jacob is wearing Esau's best clothes (verse 15). Their smell of fields and game convinces Isaac at last.

decisions.choice: a field that the LORD has blessed: the blessing begins with the land's richness
decisions.reason: Isaac's blessing starts from the scent of a fertile field and turns it into a prayer for fruitful land (verse 28). This blessing is poetry, set out in parallel lines.

decisions.choice: Esau's clothes on him
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader whose clothes Jacob is wearing (verse 15).

records.source: וְיִֽתֶּן־לְךָ֙ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים מִטַּל֙ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וּמִשְׁמַנֵּ֖י הָאָ֑רֶץ וְרֹ֥ב דָּגָ֖ן וְתִירֹֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And may give to you God of [the] dew of the heavens and of [the] fatness of the earth, and abundance of grain and new wine.
pieces: May God grant you the dew that falls from the sky and the riches of fertile soil, with grain and new wine in abundance.

L.28: And may God give you of the dew of the heavens and of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine.

R.28: May God send dew from the sky to water your land. May God make your land rich, with plenty of grain and new wine.

decisions.choice: the dew of the heavens: the moisture crops depend on
decisions.reason: In the dry summer months of Canaan, when no rain falls, the heavy night dew keeps plants alive. Dew stands for God's gift of life to the land (Deuteronomy 33:13, 28).

decisions.choice: the fatness of the earth: the richest, most fertile land
decisions.reason: "Fatness" (shemen, "oil, richness") is a picture of abundance. The same words return, with a different turn, in Esau's blessing (verse 39).

decisions.choice: grain and new wine: the main crops of the land
decisions.reason: Grain, new wine and oil sum up the harvests of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:13). Tirosh is wine fresh from the press.

records.source: יַֽעַבְד֣וּךָ עַמִּ֗ים וְיִֽשְׁתַּחֲו֤וּלְךָ֙ לְאֻמִּ֔ים הֱוֵ֤ה גְבִיר֙ לְאַחֶ֔יךָ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲוּ֥וּלְךָ֖ בְּנֵ֣י אִמֶּ֑ךָ אֹרְרֶ֣יךָ אָר֔וּר וּֽמְבָרֲכֶ֖יךָ בָּרֽוּךְ׃
records.gloss: May serve you peoples, and may bow down to you nations; be lord to your brothers, and may bow down to you [the] sons of your mother. [Those] cursing you [be] cursed, and [those] blessing you [be] blessed.
pieces: Let peoples be your servants and nations bow low before you. Rule over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow before you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed; whoever blesses you, let him be blessed."

L.29: May peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you."

R.29: May nations serve you and bow down to you. May you rule over your brothers. May your mother's sons bow down to you. May anyone who curses you be cursed, and anyone who blesses you be blessed."

decisions.choice: cursed ... blessed: God's promise to Abraham
decisions.reason: Isaac's words echo God's promise to Abraham: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse" (12:3). Without knowing it, Isaac hands on Abraham's blessing to Jacob (28:4).

decisions.choice: lord over your brothers: the younger over the older
decisions.reason: Isaac means this for Esau, but it fulfills God's word before the birth of the twins: "the older will serve the younger" (25:23). Later Edom was ruled by Israel's kings (2 Samuel 8:14).

decisions.choice: and may ... bow down: the marginal reading
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew has the verb without "and"; the Masoretes' marginal reading adds "and". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: let him be cursed ... let him be blessed
decisions.reason: The Hebrew participles are singular ("the one cursing you"); Balanced keeps the singular, which here means anyone at all.

decisions.choice: May nations serve you
decisions.reason: The verbs are wishes ("may they serve"). Readable keeps them as wishes, though in Isaac's mouth they were sure to come true (verse 33).

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר כִּלָּ֣ה יִצְחָק֮ לְבָרֵ֣ךְ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹב֒ וַיְהִ֗י אַ֣ךְ יָצֹ֤א יָצָא֙ יַעֲקֹ֔ב מֵאֵ֥ת פְּנֵ֖י יִצְחָ֣ק אָבִ֑יו וְעֵשָׂ֣ו אָחִ֔יו בָּ֖א מִצֵּידֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And it was, when had finished Isaac blessing Jacob, and it was, just had gone out Jacob from [the] presence of Isaac his father, and Esau his brother came from his hunting.
pieces: Isaac had just finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had scarcely left his father's presence, when his brother Esau came back from the hunt.

L.30: And it came about, as soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had barely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, that Esau his brother came in from his hunting.

R.30: Isaac finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob left. Just then his brother Esau came back from hunting.

decisions.choice: had barely gone out: Jacob only just escapes
decisions.reason: The doubled verb with "only" (ak yatso yatsa) stresses timing: one brother leaves as the other arrives.

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַשׂ גַּם־הוּא֙ מַטְעַמִּ֔ים וַיָּבֵ֖א לְאָבִ֑יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְאָבִ֗יו יָקֻ֤ם אָבִי֙ וְיֹאכַל֙ מִצֵּ֣יד בְּנ֔וֹ בַּעֲב֖וּר תְּבָרֲכַ֥נִּי נַפְשֶֽׁךָ׃
records.gloss: And made also he tasty food and brought [it] to his father, and he said to his father, let arise my father and eat of [the] game of his son, so that may bless me your soul.
pieces: He too made a savory dish and brought it to his father. "Sit up, Father," he said, "and eat some of your son's game, so that you can bless me."

L.31: And he too prepared tasty food and brought it to his father, and he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, so that your soul may bless me."

R.31: Esau also cooked a tasty meal and brought it to his father. He said, "Father, sit up and eat the meat I hunted. Then bless me."

decisions.choice: let my father arise: a respectful address
decisions.reason: Esau speaks of his father in the third person ("let my father arise ... his son's game"), a polite form of address to a superior.

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֛וֹ יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו מִי־אָ֑תָּה וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אֲנִ֛י בִּנְךָ֥ בְכֹֽרְךָ֖ עֵשָֽׂו׃
records.gloss: And said to him Isaac his father, who [are] you? And he said, I [am] your son, your firstborn, Esau.
pieces: "Who are you?" his father Isaac asked him. "Your son," he said, "your firstborn, Esau."

L.32: And Isaac his father said to him, "Who are you?" And he said, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."

R.32: His father Isaac asked him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am Esau, your oldest son."

records.source: וַיֶּחֱרַ֨ד יִצְחָ֣ק חֲרָדָה֮ גְּדֹלָ֣ה עַד־מְאֹד֒ וַיֹּ֡אמֶר מִֽי־אֵפ֡וֹא ה֣וּא הַצָּֽד־צַיִד֩ וַיָּ֨בֵא לִ֜י וָאֹכַ֥ל מִכֹּ֛ל בְּטֶ֥רֶם תָּב֖וֹא וָאֲבָרֲכֵ֑הוּ גַּם־בָּר֖וּךְ יִהְיֶֽה׃
records.gloss: And trembled Isaac [with] a trembling great, exceedingly, and said, who then [is] he, the one who hunted game and brought [it] to me, and I ate of all before you came, and I blessed him? Also blessed he will be.
pieces: Isaac began to shake all over. "Then who was it," he said, "that hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I gave him my blessing, and blessed he will remain!"

L.33: And Isaac trembled with a very great trembling and said, "Who then is he who hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate of it all before you came, and I blessed him? Yes, and he will be blessed."

R.33: Isaac began to shake very hard. He said, "Then who was it that hunted an animal and brought it to me? I ate it before you came, and I blessed him. Now he will always be blessed!"

decisions.choice: trembled with a very great trembling: a violent shock
decisions.reason: The verb and its noun are doubled, with "very" added: Isaac is shaken to the core. He realizes he has been deceived, and perhaps also that God's purpose (25:23) has overruled his own.

decisions.choice: he will be blessed: the blessing cannot be taken back
decisions.reason: Isaac does not withdraw the blessing even when he learns of the deceit. Spoken in God's presence (verse 7), it stands.

decisions.choice: I ate of it all: I ate everything he brought
decisions.reason: The phrase "of all" probably means Isaac ate his fill of what was brought.

records.source: כִּשְׁמֹ֤עַ עֵשָׂו֙ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֣י אָבִ֔יו וַיִּצְעַ֣ק צְעָקָ֔ה גְּדֹלָ֥ה וּמָרָ֖ה עַד־מְאֹ֑ד וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְאָבִ֔יו בָּרֲכֵ֥נִי גַם־אָ֖נִי אָבִֽי׃
records.gloss: When heard Esau [the] words of his father, and he cried out [with] a cry great and bitter, exceedingly, and said to his father, bless me, also me, my father.
pieces: When Esau heard what his father said, he let out a loud and anguished cry. "Father, bless me as well!" he begged.

L.34: When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with a very great and bitter cry, and said to his father, "Bless me, me too, my father!"

R.34: When Esau heard this, he cried out loudly in great sorrow. He said to his father, "Bless me too, Father!"

decisions.choice: a great and bitter cry: a wail of grief
decisions.reason: Tse'aqah is a cry of distress. The same phrase is used of Mordecai's cry of anguish (Esther 4:1). Esau once despised his birthright (25:34); now he grieves over the blessing.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בָּ֥א אָחִ֖יךָ בְּמִרְמָ֑ה וַיִּקַּ֖ח בִּרְכָתֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And he said, came your brother with deceit and took your blessing.
pieces: But Isaac said, "Your brother came here with a trick and carried off your blessing."

L.35: And he said, "Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing."

R.35: Isaac said, "Your brother came and tricked me. He took the blessing that was meant for you."

decisions.choice: deceit (mirmah): cunning, trickery
decisions.reason: The word appears again when Jacob complains that Laban has deceived him (29:25, the same root) and when Jacob's sons answer Shechem "with deceit" (34:13). The trickster will be tricked.

records.source: וַיֹּ֡אמֶר הֲכִי֩ קָרָ֨א שְׁמ֜וֹ יַעֲקֹ֗ב וַֽיַּעְקְבֵ֨נִי֙ זֶ֣ה פַעֲמַ֔יִם אֶת־בְּכֹרָתִ֣י לָקָ֔ח וְהִנֵּ֥ה עַתָּ֖ה לָקַ֣ח בִּרְכָתִ֑י וַיֹּאמַ֕ר הֲלֹא־אָצַ֥לְתָּ לִּ֖י בְּרָכָֽה׃
records.gloss: And he said, is it not that one called his name Jacob? And he has supplanted me these two times: my birthright he took, and look, now he has taken my blessing. And he said, have you not reserved for me a blessing?
pieces: "No wonder he is called Jacob!" Esau said. "Twice now he has gone behind my back and cheated me. First he took my birthright, and now look, he has taken my blessing too." Then he asked, "Is there no blessing left that you saved for me?"

L.36: And he said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times. He took my birthright, and look, now he has taken my blessing." And he said, "Have you not kept back a blessing for me?"

R.36: Esau said, "His name Jacob fits him well! He has cheated me two times. First he took my rights as the oldest son. Now he has taken my blessing!" Then he asked, "Do you not have any blessing left for me?"

decisions.choice: Jacob ... supplanted me (ya'qov ... ya'qeveni): a pun on Jacob's name
decisions.reason: At birth Jacob held Esau's heel (aqev), and his name was linked to it (25:26). The verb from the same root means to grab by the heel, to overreach or cheat (Jeremiah 9:4; Hosea 12:3). Esau hears in the name what Jacob has done.

decisions.choice: my birthright ... my blessing (bekhorah ... berakhah): a play on words
decisions.reason: The two words differ by the order of two letters. The birthright was the double share of the firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:17); the blessing was the father's last word. Esau sold the first (25:33), but has lost the second by trickery.

decisions.choice: No wonder he is called Jacob (B); His name Jacob fits him well (R)
alternatives: Is he not rightly named Jacob?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is a question expecting "yes"; Balanced and Readable give its force.

decisions.choice: my rights as the oldest son
decisions.reason: Readable explains the birthright in plain words.

records.source: וַיַּ֨עַן יִצְחָ֜ק וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְעֵשָׂ֗ו הֵ֣ן גְּבִ֞יר שַׂמְתִּ֥יו לָךְ֙ וְאֶת־כָּל־אֶחָ֗יו נָתַ֤תִּי לוֹ֙ לַעֲבָדִ֔ים וְדָגָ֥ן וְתִירֹ֖שׁ סְמַכְתִּ֑יו וּלְכָ֣ה אֵפ֔וֹא מָ֥ה אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֖ה בְּנִֽי׃
records.gloss: And answered Isaac and said to Esau, look, lord I have made him over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants, and [with] grain and new wine I have sustained him; and for you, then, what can I do, my son?
pieces: Isaac answered Esau, "I have already made him your master. I have given him all his relatives to serve him, and grain and new wine to keep him. So what is there left for me to do for you, my son?"

L.37: And Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Look, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants, and with grain and new wine I have sustained him. And for you, then, what can I do, my son?"

R.37: Isaac answered Esau, "I have made Jacob your master. I have said that all his relatives will serve him. I have given him plenty of grain and new wine. So what can I do for you now, my son?"

decisions.choice: I have made him ... I have given: the blessing is done
decisions.reason: Isaac speaks as if the blessing has already taken effect. What was given cannot be given twice.

decisions.choice: his brothers ... as servants: his relatives as subjects
decisions.reason: "Brothers" here means kinsmen, the peoples descended from the family. The word for servants ('avadim) means here subjects who serve a ruler, not slaves bought and owned.

decisions.choice: servants (L), to serve him (B, R)
decisions.reason: The word usually translated slave is used here of nations subject to a ruler, so a word of service is used instead.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר עֵשָׂ֜ו אֶל־אָבִ֗יו הַֽבְרָכָ֨ה אַחַ֤ת הִֽוא־לְךָ֙ אָבִ֔י בָּרֲכֵ֥נִי גַם־אָ֖נִי אָבִ֑י וַיִּשָּׂ֥א עֵשָׂ֛ו קֹל֖וֹ וַיֵּֽבְךְּ׃
records.gloss: And said Esau to his father, a blessing, one, is it to you, my father? Bless me, also me, my father. And lifted up Esau his voice and wept.
pieces: "Is that the only blessing you have, Father?" Esau said. "Bless me as well, my father!" And Esau sobbed out loud.

L.38: And Esau said to his father, "Have you only one blessing, my father? Bless me, me too, my father!" And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.

R.38: Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, Father? Please bless me too!" Then Esau cried and cried.

decisions.choice: lifted up his voice and wept: wept aloud
decisions.reason: The phrase means weeping openly and loudly (21:16; 29:11). The author of Hebrews recalls Esau's tears, which could not undo what was lost (Hebrews 12:17).

records.source: וַיַּ֛עַן יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֑יו הִנֵּ֞ה מִשְׁמַנֵּ֤י הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה מֽוֹשָׁבֶ֔ךָ וּמִטַּ֥ל הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם מֵעָֽל׃
records.gloss: And answered Isaac his father and said to him, look, away from [the] fatness of the earth will be your dwelling, and away from [the] dew of the heavens from above.
pieces: His father Isaac answered him: "Far from the rich soil of the earth you will make your home, and far from the dew of the sky above.

L.39: And Isaac his father answered and said to him, "Look, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of the heavens above.

R.39: His father Isaac answered him, "You will live far from the rich land. You will have no dew from the sky.

decisions.choice: away from the fatness ... away from the dew: Esau's land will be dry
alternatives: of the fatness ... of the dew (a lesser share of the same gifts)
decisions.reason: The same words were used in Jacob's blessing (verse 28), where "of" (min) means "some of". Here the preposition most likely means "away from": Esau's home, the rugged hills of Seir south of the Dead Sea, would be poor in fertile soil and dew. The words can also be read as a smaller share in the same gifts.

records.source: וְעַל־חַרְבְּךָ֣ תִֽחְיֶ֔ה וְאֶת־אָחִ֖יךָ תַּעֲבֹ֑ד וְהָיָה֙ כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר תָּרִ֔יד וּפָרַקְתָּ֥ עֻלּ֖וֹ מֵעַ֥ל צַוָּארֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And by your sword you will live, and your brother you will serve; and it will be, when you break loose, and you will tear off his yoke from upon your neck.
pieces: Your sword will win you your living, and you will be your brother's servant. Yet a day will come when you break loose and throw off the yoke he has laid on your neck."

L.40: And by your sword you shall live, and your brother you shall serve; and it shall come about, when you break loose, that you will tear his yoke from off your neck."

R.40: You will live by fighting, and you will serve your brother. But one day you will fight to be free, and you will no longer be under his rule."

decisions.choice: when you break loose (tarid): a rare verb
decisions.reason: The verb (rud) is rare; it seems to mean to roam or to be restless, as an animal that will not stay under the yoke. The overall sense is clear: Esau will one day throw off his brother's rule.

decisions.choice: you will tear his yoke from your neck: Edom's later freedom
decisions.reason: Edom was ruled by David (2 Samuel 8:14) and later revolted and set up its own king (2 Kings 8:20-22).

decisions.choice: by your sword you shall live: a life of raiding and war
decisions.reason: Esau's people will win their living by force rather than from rich land.

decisions.choice: you will no longer be under his rule
alternatives: you will tear off his yoke
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the yoke.

records.source: וַיִּשְׂטֹ֤ם עֵשָׂו֙ אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹ֔ב עַל־הַ֨בְּרָכָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֵּרֲכ֖וֹ אָבִ֑יו וַיֹּ֨אמֶר עֵשָׂ֜ו בְּלִבּ֗וֹ יִקְרְבוּ֙ יְמֵי֙ אֵ֣בֶל אָבִ֔י וְאַֽהַרְגָ֖ה אֶת־יַעֲקֹ֥ב אָחִֽי׃
records.gloss: And bore a grudge Esau against Jacob because of the blessing with which had blessed him his father; and said Esau in his heart, will draw near [the] days of mourning for my father, and I will kill Jacob my brother.
pieces: Esau nursed a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He told himself, "My father will soon be dead and mourned. When that time is over, I will kill my brother Jacob."

L.41: And Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him; and Esau said in his heart, "The days of mourning for my father are drawing near; then I will kill Jacob my brother."

R.41: Esau hated Jacob because their father had blessed him. Esau said to himself, "My father will die soon. When the time of mourning is over, I will kill my brother Jacob."

decisions.choice: held a grudge (satam): kept up a settled hostility
decisions.reason: The verb means to bear hatred and act on it. It is used later of Joseph's brothers fearing he will hold a grudge (50:15).

decisions.choice: said in his heart: said to himself
decisions.reason: The heart is where a person thinks and plans. Esau's plan is private, but it is soon reported (verse 42).

decisions.choice: the days of mourning for my father: the time after Isaac's death
decisions.reason: Esau will not kill his brother while their father lives. In the event Isaac lives on, and the brothers bury him together in peace (35:29).

records.source: וַיֻּגַּ֣ד לְרִבְקָ֔ה אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֥י עֵשָׂ֖ו בְּנָ֣הּ הַגָּדֹ֑ל וַתִּשְׁלַ֞ח וַתִּקְרָ֤א לְיַעֲקֹב֙ בְּנָ֣הּ הַקָּטָ֔ן וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו הִנֵּה֙ עֵשָׂ֣ו אָחִ֔יךָ מִתְנַחֵ֥ם לְךָ֖ לְהָרְגֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And were told to Rebekah [the] words of Esau her son the elder, and she sent and called for Jacob her son the younger and said to him, look, Esau your brother [is] comforting himself concerning you by killing you.
pieces: When Rebekah was told what her older son Esau was saying, she sent for her younger son Jacob and told him, "Your brother Esau is finding comfort in the thought of killing you.

L.42: And the words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah, and she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Look, Esau your brother is consoling himself about you by [planning] to kill you.

R.42: Someone told Rebekah what her older son Esau planned to do. So she sent for her younger son Jacob. She told him, "Your brother Esau is planning to kill you. That is how he is making himself feel better.

decisions.choice: consoling himself by killing you: easing his grief with plans for revenge
alternatives: planning to take revenge on you
decisions.reason: The verb (nacham) can mean to comfort oneself or to take satisfaction, even through revenge (Isaiah 1:24). Esau soothes his loss with the thought of killing Jacob.

decisions.choice: [planning]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the word that shows Esau has not yet acted.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֥ה בְנִ֖י שְׁמַ֣ע בְּקֹלִ֑י וְק֧וּם בְּרַח־לְךָ֛ אֶל־לָבָ֥ן אָחִ֖י חָרָֽנָה׃
records.gloss: And now, my son, listen to my voice and arise, flee for yourself to Laban my brother, to Haran.
pieces: Now, my son, do as I say. Leave now and escape to my brother Laban in Haran.

L.43: And now, my son, listen to my voice: arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran.

R.43: So, my son, do what I say. Run away right now to my brother Laban in Haran.

decisions.choice: Laban my brother in Haran: Rebekah's family
decisions.reason: Haran was the town in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham's family had settled (11:31) and where Abraham's servant found Rebekah (24:10, 29). Laban had welcomed the servant there (24:29-31).

records.source: וְיָשַׁבְתָּ֥ עִמּ֖וֹ יָמִ֣ים אֲחָדִ֑ים עַ֥ד אֲשֶׁר־תָּשׁ֖וּב חֲמַ֥ת אָחִֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: And remain with him some days, until turns back [the] fury of your brother,
pieces: Live with him for a short time, until your brother's rage has cooled,

L.44: And stay with him a few days, until your brother's fury turns away,

R.44: Stay with him for a short time, until your brother is not so angry with you.

decisions.choice: a few days: literally "days, ones"
decisions.reason: The phrase means a short time. Jacob stays twenty years (31:41). The same phrase is used of Jacob's seven years of work for Rachel, which seemed to him "a few days" (29:20).

records.source: עַד־שׁ֨וּב אַף־אָחִ֜יךָ מִמְּךָ֗ וְשָׁכַח֙ אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֣יתָ לּ֔וֹ וְשָׁלַחְתִּ֖י וּלְקַחְתִּ֣יךָ מִשָּׁ֑ם לָמָ֥ה אֶשְׁכַּ֛ל גַּם־שְׁנֵיכֶ֖ם י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃
records.gloss: until turns back [the] anger of your brother from you, and he forgets what you have done to him; and I will send and get you from there. Why should I be bereaved also of [the] two of you [in] one day?
pieces: until his anger toward you has gone and he has forgotten what you did to him. Then I will send word and bring you back. Must I be robbed of you both in a single day?"

L.45: until your brother's anger turns away from you and he forgets what you did to him; then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?"

R.45: When he forgets what you did to him, I will send for you to come back home. I could lose both my sons in a single day."

decisions.choice: bereaved of you both in one day: losing both sons
decisions.reason: If Esau killed Jacob, Rebekah would lose Jacob to death and Esau to the punishment for murder, whether by blood vengeance or exile (9:6; compare 2 Samuel 14:6-7).

decisions.choice: I will send and bring you from there: a promise that is never kept
decisions.reason: The story never tells of Rebekah sending for Jacob. Her death is not recorded; only her nurse's death and her burial place are mentioned (35:8; 49:31).

records.source: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר רִבְקָה֙ אֶל־יִצְחָ֔ק קַ֣צְתִּי בְחַיַּ֔י מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנ֣וֹת חֵ֑ת אִם־לֹקֵ֣חַ יַ֠עֲקֹב אִשָּׁ֨ה מִבְּנֽוֹת־חֵ֤ת כָּאֵ֨לֶּה֙ מִבְּנ֣וֹת הָאָ֔רֶץ לָ֥מָּה לִּ֖י חַיִּֽים׃
records.gloss: And said Rebekah to Isaac, I loathe my life because of [the] daughters of Heth; if takes Jacob a wife from [the] daughters of Heth like these, from [the] daughters of the land, why to me [is] life?
pieces: Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "These Hittite women make my life a misery. If Jacob also marries one of these local Hittite women, I might as well be dead."

L.46: And Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these, from the daughters of the land, what good is life to me?"

R.46: Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am sick and tired of these Hittite women that Esau married. If Jacob also marries a Hittite woman from around here, I would rather die."

decisions.choice: the daughters of Heth: Hittite women of Canaan
decisions.reason: Esau had married two Hittite women, who made life bitter for his parents (26:34-35). "Heth" is the ancestor of the Hittites living in Canaan (10:15; 23:3).

decisions.choice: Rebekah speaks to Isaac: a reason for sending Jacob away
decisions.reason: Rebekah does not tell Isaac of Esau's threat. She gives Isaac a good reason of his own to send Jacob to her family, and he does so at once (28:1-2).

decisions.choice: that Esau married
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear which Hittite women are meant (26:34).
